name: Makuria
summary: A Christian Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, in present-day Sudan. It held off the Arab armies in 652, kept a treaty (the baqt) with Egypt for about 600 years, and faded in the 14th and 15th centuries.

knownFor.label: Faras cathedral paintings
knownFor.note: Wall paintings of saints and bishops, now in Warsaw and Khartoum.

knownFor.label: Nubian archers
knownFor.note: Called the “pupil-smiters” by Arab writers for their accuracy.

knownFor.label: Baqt treaty
knownFor.note: A peace and trade agreement with Muslim Egypt that lasted centuries.

location.value: Along the Nile in northern Sudan, from the Third Cataract to around Abu Hamed; Nobatia to the north was added in the 7th century.

terrain.value: A narrow green river valley crossed by rocky cataracts and surrounded by desert.

climate.value: Very hot and dry; farming depended on the Nile flood.

resources.value: Farmland on the riverbanks, dates, cattle, gold and trade goods from Africa.

population.value: Unknown; perhaps a few hundred thousand.

urbanisation.value: Old Dongola was the main town, with churches and a palace.

disease.value: Plague reached Egypt in 1347 and may have spread into Nubia, though no source says so directly.

migration.value: Arab settlers lived in Lower Nubia from the 9th century; Bedouin Arab tribes pushed in during the 14th century.

economicBase.value: Farming irrigated with the saqiya waterwheel; herding; trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Traded with Egypt under the baqt: Nubian slaves for Egyptian wheat and cloth.

wealth.value: Prospered from trade along the Nile.

moneyAndTax.value: Mostly barter; the state never had its own currency, though Egyptian coins were common in the north.

inequality.value: Kings and bishops at the top; farmers and slaves at the bottom.

keyRulers.value: King Qalidurut (652). King Merkurios (late 7th–early 8th century). King Georgios I (9th century).

succession.value: Early writers say the throne passed from father to son; from about the 12th century it passed from a king to his sister’s son.

institutions.value: The Church, with bishops at Faras, Dongola and elsewhere; officials with Byzantine titles.

stability.value: Stable for centuries; Mamluk raids and interference from 1265, and civil wars in the 14th century.

eliteConflict.value: Rival claimants to the throne asked Egypt’s Mamluks for help.

majorWars.value: Defeated Arab invasions in 642 and 652; Mamluk invasions from the 1270s, and Mamluk-backed kings from 1311.

territoryChange.value: Annexed Nobatia to the north in the 7th century, probably in the 620s and before 642.

alliancesRivals.value: Ties to the Christian Church of Alexandria and Ethiopia; treaty partner of Muslim Egypt.

scienceEducation.value: Churches and monasteries kept Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian texts.

openness.value: Long open to trade, but defended its independence.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Nile; donkeys and camels on desert routes to Egypt and the Red Sea.

religion.value: Christianity from the 6th century (about 568 by one early account); Islam slowly spread later.

languageWriting.value: Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic, and later Arabic.

artsArchitecture.value: Churches with wall paintings (Faras), decorated pottery.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses; barley, millet and dates were the main crops.

neighbours.value: Egypt, Alodia (another Nubian kingdom to the south), Beja nomads of the eastern desert.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity from Byzantium and Egypt; later Islam.

riseSignals.value: Conversion and the defeat of Arab armies in 652 secured its independence.

declineSignals.value: Mamluk interventions, Arab migration and plague.

outcome.value: The throne hall at Dongola was a mosque by 1317; the kingdom probably collapsed in the late 15th century.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Makuria; Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002).

overallCertainty.value: Known from archaeology and Arab writers; many dates are approximate.
